speaker_role: former admissions officer (Becky Sabky, former director of international admissions and athletic-recruiting liaison at Dartmouth College, ~13 years there; previously an admissions officer at St. Lawrence University; author of a college-admissions book)
commercial_incentive: hosted by Road2College, a paid college-planning platform/membership; the webinar itself mainly gives away copies of the speaker's book rather than directly pitching a paid service on-screen
key_insights: Frames college admissions explicitly as a business: schools must balance enrollment revenue, financial aid/merit budgets, and athletic and international recruiting cycles, not just apply an 'art' or 'science.'

Because a selective school's applicant pool is already self-selected (very low performers rarely apply), few decisions are 'easy'; there is no fixed scientific formula, and readers build a case for an applicant like a lawyer building evidence for a client to present to the dean.

Describes a (discontinued) hiring exercise for prospective admissions staff: reading 3 sample fake applications in 30 minutes and picking one to admit; calls it a flawed exercise in hindsight because the real admit rate (~1 in 10) is far lower than the exercise's roughly 1-in-3 rate.

Recommends every family obtain and review their high school's 'school profile' document (from the counselor or school website), since readers pair it with the transcript to judge course rigor relative to what that specific school actually offers.

Says supplemental essays are frequently rushed or neglected relative to the personal statement, even though they can carry equal or greater weight since they show specific effort and genuine interest in that school.

On testing: describes how test-optional policies can inflate a school's reported average scores because students self-select to withhold below-average scores; advises submitting scores only if near/above a school's published average, but flags a very high test score paired with a transcript/recommendation mismatch (e.g., an 800 alongside a teacher's 'comes naturally' comment) as a red flag.

On recommendation letters: short, specific anecdotes (e.g., 'the only student I want to sit next to on the bus') are more memorable than generic praise; recommends sending only 1-2 optional additional letters, since 3+ 'smells like desperation.'

Recommends using the application's 'additional information' section -- left blank an estimated 95% of the time in her experience -- to explain any relevant context not otherwise conveyed, such as a scheduling constraint or a specific grade.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Read about 150 applications/week and roughly 12 minutes per application at peak, out of about 20,000 total applicants/year, per Becky Sabky
Dartmouth's admit rate was about 10% during much of her tenure, reportedly down to about 6% a couple years before this webinar (a few years post-pandemic), per Sabky
Hiring exercise for prospective staff involved 3 sample applications and 30 minutes, yielding about a 1-in-3 pick rate versus the real ~1-in-10 admit rate, per Sabky
Estimated about 95% of applicants leave the 'additional information' section blank, per Sabky
Served 2 years at St. Lawrence University and 13 years at Dartmouth before leaving around 2017, per Sabky
notable_or_distinctive: Describes concrete, rarely-shared operational mechanics of an elite admissions office -- the ~12-minutes-per-application reading pace and the staff hiring exercise using fake sample applications -- rather than general advice.
reliability_notes: Same speaker (Becky Sabky) as the previously summarized video 2i4lSMpG7Rk, but this is a separate, much longer live webinar interview covering substantially different and more detailed ground (business-of-admissions framing, the school profile document, the staff hiring exercise, recommendation-letter mechanics, test-optional score dynamics), so it is treated as new content rather than a repeat. She left Dartmouth admissions years before this webinar and test-optional policy began after she left, so her comments on current test-optional dynamics are outside inference rather than firsthand policy knowledge. The transcript repeatedly references audio/technical issues during the live session.
